Scanning & Skimming
Week 2.2

Scanning
• Scanning: A reading technique used for finding specific info quickly.
• Helps you learn to slip over unimportant information/words and will help
you read faster.

Scanning
• When scanning, you must have a question in mind.
• You do not read every word, but only the words that answer your question.

Simple Scanning
• We actually scan text every day, whether we know it or not.
• For example, when we read a Menu at a restaurant.
• If the waiter asks us “What would you like to drink?” we then have the
question in our head, “What do I want to drink?”
• We then quickly scan the menu for drinks while having the question “What do I
want to drink?” in mind.

Extra Notes
Scanning: Scanning involves quickly running your eyes over the text to find specific keywords, phrases, or information.
Here's how to effectively use scanning:
• Know what you're looking for: Have a clear idea of the specific information you need before you start scanning. This
could be a particular word, number, or specific details.
• Use visual cues: Scan headings, subheadings, titles, and any other formatting features that stand out. These visual
cues can guide your eyes to the relevant sections.
• Move your eyes quickly: Instead of reading every word, let your eyes move rapidly across the text. Focus on picking up
the keywords or information you're searching for.
• Ignore irrelevant details: Don't get distracted by irrelevant sentences or paragraphs. Train your eyes to skip over them
and stay focused on your target information.
• Practice reading in columns: When scanning longer texts, try reading in columns rather than reading across each line.
This allows your eyes to cover more ground quickly.
• Scanning is ideal for finding specific details, such as dates, names, or statistics, within a larger text.

Extra Notes
Skimming: Skimming involves quickly glancing over a text to get a general idea of its content without reading every word. Skimming is
particularly useful when you want to determine if a text is relevant or worth reading in detail. Here are some skimming techniques to
employ:
• Read the title and subtitles: Titles and subtitles provide a quick summary of the main ideas or topics covered in the text.
• Read the first and last sentences of paragraphs: These often contain the main points or conclusions. By reading these sentences, you
can gain a sense of the overall content.
• Look for keywords and phrases: Scan for keywords and phrases that stand out. They can give you a sense of the text's main focus or
subject matter.
• Pay attention to formatting: Bold or italicized text, bullet points, and highlighted sections often indicate important or emphasized
information. Skim through these parts to grasp the key points.
• Observe the structure: Look at the organization of the text, such as headings, subheadings, and paragraphs. This can help you
understand the overall structure and flow of ideas.
• Skimming allows you to quickly determine the main ideas, tone, and relevance of a text without investing extensive time.

Scanning & Skimming
Both scanning and skimming techniques require practice to become
efficient. They are not meant to replace in-depth reading, but rather to aid
you in quickly obtaining specific information or deciding if a text is worth a
more thorough read.

Pre-Reading
• Preparation for the act of
reading.
• There are 4 steps to PreReading.
1- Preview
2- Predict
3- Prior-Knowledge
4- Purpose

Previewing
Taking a quick look
at the reading before
trying to understand
the material or text.
Ask yourself, if the
text is based on
reality, true events,
or a creative story.

If the text is fiction vs non-fiction
Fiction:
• Look at the title, chapter headings, introductory notes, and illustrations.
Non-fiction:
• Look at the text features, captions, and illustrations to determine the subject matter and to
recall prior knowledge to decide what you know about the topic.
Previewing also helps you figure out what you already know about the text and what you do not know.

Predicting
Building anticipation for what happens next is any easy
way to make reading fun.
It keeps you excited and makes you wonder what might
happen next.
Look at clues and hints of the things you read to make
predictions.
Common questions to ask yourself when predicting:
- What will the book/text be about?
- Who will the main characters be?
- What big events will happen in the story?
- Where will the events take place?
- What important information can I gather?

Prior Knowledge
Things you know about the subject
before you begin reading a new text.
Could be something you studied before,
or prior experience related to the subject.

Purpose
• Figuring out an author’s purpose will help you
understand what you read.
• What is the purpose?
To entertain? To persuade? To raise inform?
What is his/her intention?

More Advanced Form of Pre-Reading
1. Previewing: Take a few minutes to scan the text before reading it in detail. Look at the headings, subheadings, bolded or italicized text, and any
other formatting features that stand out. Read the first and last paragraphs of each section or chapter to get a general sense of the content.
2. Activating prior knowledge: Reflect on what you already know about the topic or subject matter. Consider any related experiences, facts, or
concepts that might help you connect with the material. This helps you establish a foundation and make connections as you read.
3. Setting goals: Identify your purpose for reading. Are you reading for information, entertainment, or analysis? Knowing your goals will help you
approach the text with the right mindset and focus on the relevant details.
4. Predicting: Make predictions about what you expect to encounter in the text. Look at the title, headings, and any visual aids to form hypotheses
about the content. This activates your curiosity and prepares you to search for specific information as you read.
5. Previewing vocabulary: Look for unfamiliar words or terms in the text. Take note of them and try to understand their meanings before you start
reading. This can involve looking up definitions, using context clues, or consulting a dictionary or glossary.
6. Formulating questions: Generate questions based on the title, headings, or any other cues in the text. These questions can guide your reading and
help you stay engaged. As you read, seek answers to your questions and adjust or add new questions as needed.

Keywords
• Keywords are specific words or phrases that carry significant meaning and
represent the main ideas or concepts within a text. These are the words that
often convey essential information or are central to the topic being
discussed. Here are a few key points about keywords:

Keywords
1. Importance: Keywords are important because they help convey the main ideas and focus of a text. They act as a bridge between the writer's intention and the reader's understanding.
2. Identification: Keywords can be identified by their relevance to the topic or subject matter being discussed. They are often
repeated throughout the text and carry a higher degree of significance compared to other words.
3. Information retrieval: Keywords are useful for searching and retrieving specific information from a text or a larger body
of written work. When using search engines or databases, entering relevant keywords increases the chances of finding
accurate and relevant results.
4. Contextual significance: The meaning and importance of keywords can vary depending on the context. A keyword in
one text may have a different connotation or significance in another. It's important to consider the surrounding content to
fully understand the intended meaning of a keyword.
5. Different types: Keywords can take various forms, including single words, phrases, or compound terms. They can be
nouns, verbs, adjectives, or even specific names and dates. The type of keywords used depends on the nature of the text
and the specific information being conveyed.

Annotation
Annotation refers to the act of adding additional information or notes to a text, image, or any other
form of data. It involves the process of highlighting, commenting, or marking specific elements within a
document or dataset to provide clarification, context, or analysis.
Annotations can serve various purposes, depending on the context:
1. Text Annotation: In textual documents, annotations can be used to provide explanations,
definitions, references, or translations for specific words, phrases, or passages. These annotations
are often found in academic texts, literature, or scholarly research.
2. Image Annotation: In the context of images, annotation involves adding labels, markers, or
descriptions to specific regions or objects within the image. This can be used for various purposes
such as object recognition, image classification, or training machine learning algorithms.
3. Data Annotation: Data annotation involves labeling or marking data points in datasets to indicate
specific attributes, categories, or classifications. This is particularly relevant in machine learning
and AI applications, where labeled data is used to train models for tasks like object detection,
sentiment analysis, or speech recognition.
4. Audio Annotation: Audio annotation involves adding tags, timestamps, or transcriptions to audio
files. This helps in tasks like speech-to-text conversion, speaker identification, or audio data
analysis.
• Annotations can be performed manually by humans or through automated processes using
machine learning algorithms. They play a crucial role in organizing and understanding data,
enabling effective analysis, knowledge extraction, and training of AI models.
